terms.grammar: pronoun; in classical Latin gen. nūllīus, abl. nūllō
evidence: Varr. RR 2.1.2: nēmō enim omnia potest scīre
terms.comment: Of persons only; for things, nihil (see nothing). Nēmō nostrum, none of us (see none); nēmō nōn, everybody (see everyone). Lewis & Short: classical Latin takes the genitive and ablative from nūllus.

terms.gloss: no (person); nobody, in the cases nēmō lacks
evidence: Sen. Ep. 3.4: et omnibus crēdere et nūllī
terms.comment: Supplies the missing cases of nēmō (nūllīus, nūllō), and as an adjective agrees with its noun: nūllus amīcus, no friend (see no).

evidence: Cic. Sen. 21: nec vērō quemquam senem audīvī oblītum quō locō thēsaurum obruisset
terms.comment: Where a sentence goes on with “and nobody”, Latin joins with nec and uses quisquam (see and not, someone).

phrases.latin: ita Canīniō cōnsule scītō nēminem prandisse
phrases.english: so, in Caninius’s consulship, let me tell you, nobody had lunch

phrases.latin: itaque nēmō adhūc convenīre mē voluit, cui fuerim occupātus
phrases.english: and so far nobody who wanted to see me has found me busy

phrases.latin: Nēmō timendō ad summum pervenit locum.
phrases.english: Nobody ever reached the top by being afraid.

sources: Lewis & Short: nemo · Lewis & Short: nullus · Lewis & Short: quisquam
